header: \post{Every Cause Wants To Be A Cult}{Eliezer Yudkowsky}{2007}{https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/yEjaj7PWacno5EvWa/every-cause-wants-to-be-a-cult}
notes: \cpara{Reports The Register's allegations accurately, and marks them as allegations. The same article reports that the wrongly banned user was reinstated ``after a mere 75 minutes,'' that the administrator gave up her powers, and that the Arbitration Committee admonished her. The post's one case of a noble cause turning cultish is also a case of its members pushing back, which the post does not mention.}
\cpara{Raises, in order to reject it, the view that the cause itself breeds the fault.}
\cpara{Applies ``Correspondence Bias'' (June 2007): explain the behavior by ordinary human nature, not by an unusual disposition of the people involved.}
\cpara{The thesis. That in-group bias is part of human nature is common ground. That, given human adherents, ``Everything else follows naturally,'' is the claim the post needs, and it is asserted.}

\cpara{Supports the thesis with analogies: heat evens out, programs gather patches. An analogy can picture a tendency; it cannot show that human groups have one. ``High-entropy state'' and ``attractor'' restate the claim in the words of physics without adding evidence, as in ``The Bottom Line.''}

\cpara{The claim in its widest form: every group with an unusual goal drifts toward cultishness ``unless they make a constant effort to resist it.'' The support is two cases, Wikipedia and, next, the Objectivists. The post does not say what counts as the effort, so it names no case that could count against the claim.}

\cpara{Applies the point to the author's own side: calling the cause ``rationality'' protects nothing, and probability theory is to be used, not joined as an in-group. The group, the Objectivists, is named only in the footnote.}
\cfact{The two posts cited here appeared on 15 and 18 December 2007, after this one, so the footnote was added in a later revision.}

\cpara{Makes cultishness a matter of degree, with science as the test case. The example is a set of questions, not findings. Evidence on the first question existed: in a 1982 study, twelve articles were resubmitted to the journals that had published them, under fictitious names and institutions; of the nine not detected, ``eight of the nine were rejected'' (Peters and Ceci, \textsc{Behavioral and Brain Sciences}). The authors weighed several interpretations.}
\cpara{Explains the choice of example: it points to a place where cultishness can be measured and pushed back, not to a vague charge.}

\cpara{Says what the essay does not do, and restates its two points: a worthy cause needs no less effort, and naming its battle lines does not betray it. The engine comparison illustrates the second point.}
\cpara{Ends by turning the correspondence-bias point of the third paragraph into a warning: whoever thinks cults are made of ``mutants'' will not make the effort.}
